title: Digital Skills for Work
tagline: Find real jobs, apply online and work with digital tools.
description: More and more jobs are advertised and applied for online. This course shows you where to find real vacancies, how to avoid fake offers, how to write a CV and apply by email from your phone, and how to handle online interviews and simple workplace tools.
outcomes: Find job adverts in trusted places
Write a CV and cover letter on your phone
Send a complete application by email
Use shared documents and simple spreadsheets

modules.title: Finding work online
modules.summary: Where real jobs are advertised and how to spot fake ones.

lessons.title: Where to find real jobs
lessons.body:
Jobs in Zambia are advertised in many places. Looking in several of them gives you more chances.

## Good places to look
- **Newspapers**, in print and on their official websites and Facebook pages. Many employers still advertise there.
- **Company websites and official social media pages.** Look for a page called *Careers* or *Vacancies*.
- **Government vacancies**, announced by the hiring ministry or public body on its official pages and in newspapers.
- **Job websites and apps**, including LinkedIn. Create a simple profile so employers can find you.
- **NGOs and international organisations**, which list jobs on their own websites.
- **Community notice boards**, churches, ICT hubs and word of mouth. Many jobs are never advertised online.

## Read the advert carefully
A real advert usually says:

- the job title and the employer's name,
- what the job involves and what you need (qualifications, experience),
- how to apply, and the **closing date**.

Note the closing date and apply early.

## Set up alerts
Many job sites can send you an email when a new job matches your search. Use the words that describe the work you want, like *driver*, *accounts clerk* or *shop assistant*, and your town.

## Keep a list
Write down each job you apply for: the employer, the date, and how you applied. When someone calls you, you will know which job it is.
key_points: Look in several places, online and offline
A real advert names the employer and a closing date
Keep a list of the jobs you apply for
lessons.try_it: Find one real job advert today and write down its closing date.

lessons.title: Spotting fake job offers
lessons.body:
Fake job adverts are one of the most common scams. They target people who need work, and can cost money you cannot afford to lose.

## Warning signs
- **You must pay** for something: an application fee, medical, training, uniform, travel or a "processing fee". Real employers do not charge you to get a job.
- **Very high pay** for easy work or no experience.
- **No interview**, or only a short chat on WhatsApp.
- The contact is a personal Gmail or WhatsApp number, not a company address.
- Pressure: *"Only three places left, pay today."*
- They ask for your **NRC, bank details or mobile money PIN** before any interview.
- Jobs abroad that promise visas, flights and housing for a fee.

## Check the employer
- Search the company name online. Does it have a real website and address?
- Call the company on a number you find yourself, not the one in the advert, and ask if the job is real.
- Ask people who work in that field.

## Jobs abroad
Work abroad offers can lead to people being trapped or exploited. Be very careful. Check the agency with the authorities, never hand over your passport to an agent, and tell your family exactly where you are going.

## If you are unsure, do not pay
If an offer asks for money first, stop. A real job will still be there after you check.
key_points: Real employers never charge you to get a job
Check the company on a number you find yourself
Be very careful with job offers abroad
lessons.try_it: Search online for one company you would like to work for and find its official contact details.

lessons.title: Researching an employer
lessons.body:
Before you apply, and especially before an interview, find out about the employer. It helps you decide if the job is right and impresses the interviewer.

## What to look for
- **What they do:** their products, services or mission.
- **Where they work:** their offices, branches or projects.
- **Recent news:** a new branch, a project, an award.
- **Their values:** many organisations list them on an *About us* page.

## Where to look
- The organisation's **official website**, especially the About, News and Careers pages.
- Their **Facebook or LinkedIn page**.
- News stories. Search the organisation's name and look at the News tab.
- People who work there, or used to.

## Use what you learn
- In your **cover letter**, mention one thing you know: *"I admire your work training young farmers in Southern Province."*
- In an **interview**, when asked *"Why do you want to work here?"*, you will have a real answer.
- Prepare one or two questions to ask them, like *"What does a normal day look like in this role?"*

## Spot problems early
If you cannot find anything about an employer, or what you find does not match the advert, be careful. It may be a fake job.

## Save your notes
Keep short notes on your phone for each employer you research. Read them again before the interview.
key_points: Read the employer's About and News pages
Mention something you learned in your application
If you can find nothing about them, be careful
lessons.try_it: Pick one employer and write three facts about them in your phone's notes.

modules.title: Your CV and application
modules.summary: CV, cover letter and sending it all by email.

lessons.title: Writing a CV on your phone
lessons.body:
A **CV** (curriculum vitae) is a short document that tells an employer who you are, what you can do and how to contact you.

## Use a free app
Install **Google Docs** from the Play Store. Tap **+**, then **Choose template**, and pick a résumé template. Replace the example text with yours.

## What to include
1. **Name and contact details:** phone, email and town. You do not need your NRC number, marital status or a photo unless asked.
2. **Profile:** two or three sentences about you. *"Hard-working shop assistant with three years of experience serving customers and handling cash."*
3. **Work experience:** most recent first. Employer, job title, dates, and two or three things you did.
4. **Education:** school or college, qualification, year.
5. **Skills:** languages you speak (English, Bemba, Nyanja, Tonga...), computer skills, driving licence.
6. **References:** two people who can speak about your work, with their permission. Or write *Available on request*.

## Volunteer work and small jobs count
Selling at the market, helping in church, volunteering or caring for family all show skills. Include them.

## Keep it short and clean
One or two pages. Clear headings. No spelling mistakes. Ask someone to read it.

## Save as PDF
In Google Docs, tap the three dots, **Share and export**, **Save as**, and choose **PDF**. Name it *Firstname_Lastname_CV.pdf*.
key_points: Use a Google Docs template
Put your most recent work first
Save and send your CV as a PDF
lessons.try_it: Open Google Docs and start your CV from a template.

lessons.title: Writing a short cover letter
lessons.body:
A **cover letter** is a short letter that goes with your CV. It explains why you want this job and why you are a good fit. Some employers read it first.

## A simple shape
**Greeting:** *Dear Hiring Manager,* or the person's name if the advert gives it.

**Paragraph 1: the job.** *I am writing to apply for the post of Receptionist advertised on your website on 3 November.*

**Paragraph 2: why you fit.** Choose two or three things from the advert and show you have them.
*In my two years at Mwila Pharmacy, I welcomed customers, answered calls and kept the appointment book. I speak English, Bemba and Nyanja.*

**Paragraph 3: why this employer.** *I admire your clinic's work in the community and would be proud to be part of your team.*

**Closing:** *Thank you for considering my application. I am available for an interview at any time.* Then *Yours faithfully* (if you used Dear Sir/Madam) or *Yours sincerely* (if you used a name), and your name and phone number.

## Tips
- Write a new letter for each job. Copying the same letter shows.
- Keep it under one page.
- Match the words used in the advert.
- Check the employer's name and the job title carefully.

## In an email
When applying by email, your cover letter can be the email message itself, with your CV attached. Some employers ask for it as a separate PDF. Follow what the advert says.
key_points: Say which job, why you fit, and why this employer
Write a new letter for each job
Keep it under one page
lessons.try_it: Write a cover letter for a job you would like, using the shape in this lesson.

lessons.title: Sending an application by email
lessons.body:
Many employers ask you to apply by email. A complete, tidy email makes a good first impression.

## Before you send
- Read the advert again. What exactly do they ask for? CV, cover letter, certificates, references?
- Is there a **reference number** for the job? Include it.
- Prepare all documents as **PDFs** with clear names.

## Writing the email
**To:** the exact address in the advert.

**Subject:** the job title and reference, for example *Application: Accounts Clerk (Ref AC/24/11)*.

**Message:**
*Dear Sir/Madam,*

*Please find attached my application for the post of Accounts Clerk (Ref AC/24/11), as advertised on 1 November. I have attached my CV, cover letter and certificates.*

*Thank you for your time. I look forward to hearing from you.*

*Yours faithfully,*
*Mutale Banda*
*097...*

## Attach and check
1. Tap the **paper clip** and add each file.
2. Check every file opened and is the right one.
3. Check the email address, subject and spelling.
4. Tap **Send**.

## After sending
- Look in your **Sent** folder to confirm it went.
- Note the date in your job list.
- Check your inbox, and the **Spam** folder, every day.
- If you hear nothing after two weeks, a short polite follow-up email is fine.
key_points: Follow exactly what the advert asks for
Use the job title and reference in the subject
Check Sent, Inbox and Spam afterwards
lessons.try_it: Write an application email to yourself with your CV attached, and check it arrives.

quiz.explanation: A letter for each job shows real interest.

modules.title: Interviews and tools at work
modules.summary: Online interviews, shared documents and spreadsheets.

lessons.title: Preparing for an online interview
lessons.body:
Interviews are often held by **video call** on Zoom, Google Meet, Teams or WhatsApp. Good preparation makes you calm and confident.

## The day before
- Install the app named in the invitation and test it with a friend.
- Check you have enough **data**, or arrange to use Wi-Fi. An hour of video uses a lot.
- Charge your phone, and have a charger or power bank ready in case of load-shedding.
- Read your notes about the employer and your CV again.

## Your space
- A **quiet place** where you will not be disturbed. Tell your family.
- **Light in front of you**, like a window, not behind you.
- A plain background.
- Rest the phone on something steady at **eye level**. Do not hold it in your hand.

## Dress and manner
Dress as you would for an in-person interview. Join **5 minutes early**. Smile, look at the camera when you speak, and speak clearly.

## Common questions
Practise short answers to:
- *Tell us about yourself.* (Work, skills, what you want next. One minute.)
- *Why do you want this job?*
- *Tell us about a problem you solved.*
- *Do you have any questions for us?* Always have one ready.

## If the connection fails
Stay calm. Rejoin using the same link. If it keeps failing, turn off your video, or send a short message to the interviewer explaining and asking to continue by phone.
key_points: Test the app and your data the day before
Quiet place, light in front of you, phone at eye level
Practise answers to common questions
lessons.try_it: Practise answering 'Tell us about yourself' out loud in one minute.

lessons.title: Working on shared documents
lessons.body:
At work, people often write documents together online with **Google Docs** or **Microsoft Word**. Everyone sees the same document and changes appear straight away.

## Opening a shared document
Someone sends you a **link** by email or WhatsApp. Tap it. It opens in the Google Docs app or your browser. You may need to sign in with your Gmail account.

## What you can do
Depending on what the owner allows, you can:

- **View:** read only.
- **Comment:** add notes without changing the text.
- **Edit:** change the text directly.

## Adding a comment
1. Press and hold on a word to select it.
2. Tap **Comment** (a speech bubble with a +).
3. Type your note, like *Should this say 15 learners?*, and tap send.

Comments are a polite way to suggest changes in someone else's work.

## Suggesting changes
In Google Docs you can switch to **Suggesting** mode. Your changes show in colour, and the owner can accept or reject them. This is good when editing a manager's document.

## Version history
Every change is saved automatically. If something goes wrong, the owner can open **Version history** and go back to an earlier version.

## Good habits
- Do not delete other people's work. Comment instead.
- Write your name next to sections you are responsible for.
- Do not share a work document link outside your team.
key_points: Shared documents update for everyone at once
Use comments to suggest changes politely
Every change is saved automatically
lessons.try_it: Create a Google Doc, share it with a friend, and ask them to add a comment.

lessons.title: Simple spreadsheets for work
lessons.body:
A **spreadsheet** is a grid of boxes for lists and numbers, like stock, sales, attendance or a budget. **Google Sheets** is free on your phone.

## The grid
- **Columns** go down and have letters: A, B, C.
- **Rows** go across and have numbers: 1, 2, 3.
- Each box is a **cell**, named by its column and row, like **B2**.

## Making a simple list
1. Open Google Sheets and tap **+** to make a new sheet.
2. In row 1, type headings: *Date* in A1, *Item* in B1, *Amount* in C1.
3. Fill in one row for each entry below.

## Adding up automatically
Tap the empty cell under your amounts, for example **C10**, and type:

**=SUM(C2:C9)**

Press enter. The sheet adds all the amounts from C2 to C9. When you change a number, the total updates itself.

## Other useful formulas
- **=AVERAGE(C2:C9)** finds the average.
- **=C2*D2** multiplies two cells, like quantity times price.

## Tips
- Keep one kind of information per column.
- Put dates in a consistent way, like 05/11/2026.
- Freeze the heading row: select row 1, tap the three dots, **Freeze**.

Spreadsheets are a skill many employers ask for. Even simple lists show you can work with data.
key_points: Columns have letters, rows have numbers
=SUM(C2:C9) adds a list of numbers
One kind of information per column
lessons.try_it: Make a sheet of five things you bought this week and add a total with =SUM.

quiz.question: A 'job' offer from abroad asks you to pay for a visa through an agent and hand over your passport. What should you do?

quiz.explanation: Overseas job scams can trap people. Check first and keep your passport.

Take a blurry photo of it
quiz.explanation: A clearly named PDF looks professional and opens anywhere.
